minimal_context: The class is standing in a circle for a group reading activity to figure out the meaning of a text extract about a battle at the gates of Troy.
dialogue:
TUTOR: Everyone, please stand in a circle. We are going to read this text extract about what might be happening in a battle at the gates of Troy.

STUDENT: (Slouches on a chair in the corner instead of joining the circle)

TUTOR: Let's figure out the meaning together. What do you think it means when the text says he was 'struck him on the ear'?

STUDENT: He hit him hard on the ear.

TUTOR: Okay. Now we are going to take turns reading one phrase at a time. Here is the book, it is your turn to read.

STUDENT: (Becomes angry and hostile when the book is given to him, unable to sound out the words)

options.A: Implement genuine multicultural curricula that address race and disability, acknowledge the student's realities, and treat the student as a respected source of knowledge during the reading activity.
options.B: Highlight high-quality reading miscues with praise, focus on the miscues that affect the meaning-making process, and do not count the student's dialect variations as reading errors.
options.C: Enhance the student's self-regulation by using argumentation and dialogue during the reading activity, rather than trying to quell the student's arguments or hostility.
options.D: Establish a rule that anyone can say "stop" to ask about a word's meaning, figure out the meaning together, and note when you yourself do not know a name.
